routing_rationale: 9-year Padlet veteran, NUS CompEng (same school as Nitesh). Sole Engineering Manager, manages 22 engineers — the de facto engineering head below the founder. Hands-in-code per GitHub badges. Distinct angle: engineering execution and content-moderation specifically — the structural difference between Sandbox (had user accounts as moderation enforcement hooks) and Arcade (no student login, no enforcement hooks). Distinct from Nitesh (architectural compliance), Audrey (operational queue), Collin (product-level documentation).

research_summary.trigger_event: Linh publicly stated content moderation as a top engineering priority in the tldraw Sandbox case study (April 2025): 'Content moderation was one of the more important features since we want Sandbox to be safe for use for children in classrooms.' Arcade launched early 2026 with no student login by design — the same moderation problem at higher difficulty because the policy-enforcement surface that user accounts gave Sandbox isn't there.
research_summary.key_insight: Anchored on his publicly stated Sandbox priority — paraphrased in the email rather than quoted verbatim, since vendor-case-study quotes are intentional public statements but quoting them back can still feel like leveraging marketing. Did not pitch security infrastructure (CSPM/IAM) — he's frontend-mobile by training, not security. CTA was specifically reframed (v1 had an SRE-plumbing question 'model-side logs only, or also platform-side correlation?' — wrong altitude for a frontend-mobile EM whose stated priority is product-level moderation; v2 reframed to 'What does measurement look like for Arcade moderation right now?').

draft.body:
Sandbox shipped with content moderation as a top-priority engineering feature because user accounts gave you natural enforcement hooks. Arcade lands at a separate domain with no student login by design — same moderation problem, structurally harder because the policy-enforcement surface that Sandbox had isn't there.

Where it gets hard isn't the moderation decision itself — it's reconstructing what happened when something slips through, since without accounts the trace lives only across model inputs, outputs, and the request context around them.

Transilience treats that trace as something the platform produces continuously, not assembled when an incident review starts.

What does measurement look like for Arcade moderation right now?
draft.architecture: signal-to-question — paraphrases his publicly stated Sandbox priority without quoting verbatim, names the structural difference for Arcade (no enforcement hooks), names the engineer-relevant problem (reconstructing what happened across model + request context), one product sentence, one product-level engineering question

verdict_history.reason: CTA at wrong altitude — SRE-plumbing question to a frontend-mobile EM. 'Whatever the model returned' too casual. 'The gap that opens up' was a diagnostic move appearing in three of four Padlet drafts.
CTA reframed to product-level measurement question. Casualness replaced with 'request context around them' — precise. 'Where it gets hard' replaces 'The gap that opens up' — different syntactic move.

witness.what_works: Anchors on his publicly stated Sandbox priority without quoting verbatim — earns observational ground without surveillance frame. Names the structural difference (Arcade has no accounts, therefore no enforcement hooks) that he would recognize as exactly his problem. Product sentence matches his frame (audit trail / incident review / continuous platform output). CTA is product-level, not infra-level — right altitude.
witness.what_fails: The 'reconstructing what happened when something slips through' framing assumes content does sometimes slip through. For an EM proud of Sandbox's moderation, this could feel slightly accusatory. Acceptable because (a) any honest engineer building AI moderation knows nothing is 100%, (b) the framing is structural ('when something slips') not specific ('your moderation has failed').
